questions.content:
Hospital microbiologists are studying a bacterium that causes wound infections. A culture starts with 500 bacterial cells in a nutrient broth kept at 37 °C. Under these conditions each cell divides once every 20 minutes. The microbiologists then spread the bacteria on agar plates and place small paper discs soaked in different antibiotics on each plate. After 24 hours they measure the diameter of the clear zone around each disc.

Antibiotic A: clear zone diameter 22 mm
Antibiotic B: clear zone diameter 14 mm
Antibiotic C: no clear zone (0 mm)

(a) State the type of asexual reproduction used by bacteria. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the number of bacterial cells in the broth after 2 hours, assuming no cells die. Show your working. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the area of the clear zone around the disc of antibiotic A. Use area = πr² and give your answer to the nearest mm². (2 marks)
(d) Explain why no bacteria grew inside the clear zones. (2 marks)
(e) Antibiotic C was used heavily in the hospital last year. Predict what has happened to the bacterial population and justify your prediction using natural selection. (2 marks)
(f) Explain why antibiotics would not be a suitable treatment for an infection caused by a virus. (2 marks)

(Total 11 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Binary fission (do not accept: mitosis, budding, meiosis)
(b) [1] 2 hours = 120 minutes, so 6 divisions (120 ÷ 20), giving 500 × 2^6
[1] 32 000 cells (ECF: correct use of their number of divisions, for example 5 divisions gives 16 000 for 1 mark)
(c) [1] Radius = 11 mm and area = π × 11²
[1] 380 mm² (accept 380.1; ECF for a wrong radius. Using diameter 22 as the radius gives 1521 mm², which scores the method mark only)
(d) [1] The antibiotic diffused out of the disc into the agar
[1] It killed the bacteria or stopped them growing or dividing (accept: damaged cell walls or prevented cell wall formation)
(e) [1] Prediction: the population is now mostly or entirely resistant to antibiotic C (accept: antibiotic C no longer works)
[1] Justification: a few bacteria with a resistance mutation survived the antibiotic, reproduced and passed the allele on, so the resistant proportion increased over generations (natural selection)
(f) [1] Viruses are not cells and have no cell wall or cell machinery for the antibiotic to target
[1] Viruses reproduce inside host cells, where antibiotics do not act (accept: antibiotics target bacteria only)
Common errors: saying bacteria 'become immune' or 'get used to' the antibiotic as individuals; saying the bacteria 'decided' to mutate; confusing the clear zone diameter with the radius.

questions.content:
A biotechnology company is developing a fermentation process in which yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. A technician mixed 5 g of dried yeast with 100 cm³ of glucose solution at 35 °C and collected the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe for 10 minutes. The experiment was repeated three times for each glucose concentration.

Volume of carbon dioxide collected in 10 minutes (cm³)
Glucose concentration 5%: trial 1 = 12, trial 2 = 14, trial 3 = 13. Mean = to be calculated
Glucose concentration 10%: trial 1 = 25, trial 2 = 27, trial 3 = 26. Mean = 26
Glucose concentration 15%: trial 1 = 36, trial 2 = 38, trial 3 = 40. Mean = 38
Glucose concentration 20%: trial 1 = 37, trial 2 = 39, trial 3 = 38. Mean = 38

(a) Calculate the mean volume of carbon dioxide for the 5% glucose solution. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the mean rate of carbon dioxide production, in cm³ per minute, for the 10% glucose solution. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in mean volume of carbon dioxide when the glucose concentration rises from 5% to 10%. (2 marks)
(d) Describe the pattern shown by the means as glucose concentration increases from 5% to 20%. (2 marks)
(e) Explain the pattern between 15% and 20% glucose. (2 marks)
(f) Evaluate how reliable these results are. (3 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 13 cm³ ((12 + 14 + 13) ÷ 3)
(b) [1] 26 ÷ 10 (volume divided by time in minutes)
[1] 2.6 cm³ per minute (units needed)
(c) [1] (26 − 13) ÷ 13 × 100 (ECF from their answer to (a))
[1] 100% (accept: doubled)
(d) [1] The volume rises as glucose concentration increases from 5% to 15% (accept: positive relationship, about +13 cm³ per 5%)
[1] Between 15% and 20% it levels off or plateaus, with no further increase (38 cm³ at both)
(e) [1] Another factor has become limiting, for example the number of yeast cells or the amount or activity of their enzymes
[1] All enzyme active sites are already occupied or working at maximum speed, so extra glucose cannot be used faster (accept: yeast is saturated)
(f) [1] Ranges are small (2, 2, 4 and 2 cm³), so the repeats agree closely, which supports reliability
[1] The 15% results have the widest range (4 cm³), so there is some variation, possibly from temperature or mixing differences
[1] Only three repeats were done; more repeats would improve reliability; judgement stated (for example: fairly reliable but could be improved)
Common errors: describing the plateau as 'the reaction stopped'; giving the rate without units; calculating the percentage change using the new value as the denominator (this gives 50%).

questions.content:
An ecologist is estimating populations in a meadow that is 40 m long and 25 m wide. She counts a wildflower species in ten 1 m² quadrats.

Number of plants per quadrat: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 2, 6

She also studies a ground beetle. She catches 40 beetles, marks each with a small dot of non-toxic paint on the underside of the wing case, and releases them. Two days later she catches a second sample of 50 beetles. Of these, 8 are marked.

(a) Calculate the mean number of plants per quadrat. (1 mark)
(b) Use your answer to (a) to estimate the total number of plants in the meadow. Show your working. (2 marks)
(c) State two ways the ecologist can avoid bias when placing the quadrats. (2 marks)
(d) Estimate the beetle population using population = (first sample × second sample) ÷ marked in second sample. (2 marks)
(e) Identify two assumptions that must be true for the beetle estimate to be valid. (2 marks)
(f) The meadow has many different species of plants and insects. Explain why high biodiversity can make an ecosystem more stable. (3 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 4 plants per quadrat (40 ÷ 10)
(b) [1] Meadow area = 40 × 25 = 1000 m²
[1] 4 × 1000 = 4000 plants (ECF from (a))
(c) [1] Use random coordinates or a random number generator to choose positions
[1] Use a large enough number of quadrats or cover the whole meadow (accept: do not choose by eye or only in dense areas)
(d) [1] (40 × 50) ÷ 8
[1] 250 beetles
(e) [1] Marked beetles mix evenly back into the population and the marking does not change their survival or chance of being recaught
[1] No significant births, deaths, immigration or emigration between the two samples (accept: marks do not wear off)
(f) [1] Many species means many food sources and many links in food webs
[1] If one species declines, others can replace its role, so consumers still have food
[1] This keeps energy flow and populations steady, so the ecosystem recovers more easily from disturbance (accept: greater genetic variation gives resilience to disease or climate change)
Common errors: multiplying the mean by the number of quadrats (10) instead of the meadow area; using 40 × 8 ÷ 50 in the beetle formula; saying more species 'always' means more animals.

questions.content:
Amylase is an enzyme in human saliva that breaks down starch into sugars. A student wants to investigate how the pH of the surrounding solution affects the activity of amylase. She has the following materials: 1% starch solution, 1% amylase solution, buffer solutions at pH 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, iodine solution, a white tile with wells, test tubes, a water bath set to 35 °C, a stopwatch, graduated pipettes and a thermometer. Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present and stays orange-brown when starch is absent.

(a) Write a testable hypothesis for this investigation and give the scientific reasoning behind it. (2 marks)
(b) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable. (2 marks)
(c) State three variables that must be controlled and explain how each will be controlled. (3 marks)
(d) Design a method the student could follow, with enough detail that another student could repeat it. Include how she will measure the dependent variable and how she will make the results reliable. (4 marks)
(e) Describe one safety precaution and one ethical consideration for this investigation. (2 marks)
(f) State how the student should present and process her results to identify the optimum pH. (1 mark)

(Total 14 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Testable hypothesis stating a relationship, for example: amylase will break down starch fastest at about pH 7 and more slowly at lower and higher pH
[1] Reasoning: extreme pH changes the shape of the active site (denatures the enzyme), so the substrate no longer fits; saliva is near neutral so amylase is adapted to about pH 7
(b) [1] Independent variable: pH of the buffer solution
[1] Dependent variable: time taken for the starch to disappear, or the time for iodine to stop turning blue-black (accept: rate of starch breakdown)
(c) [1] Temperature, controlled by a water bath at 35 °C checked with a thermometer
[1] Volume and concentration of amylase and starch, controlled by measuring the same volume of each with a pipette from the same stock solutions
[1] Volume of buffer or time and method of sampling, controlled by using the same volume and testing at the same intervals (any third valid variable with a method; mark each correct variable with its control, maximum 3)
(d) [1] Clear steps: put starch and a buffer in a test tube, place in the 35 °C bath, add amylase and start the stopwatch
[1] Every 30 seconds remove a drop and test it with iodine on the tile
[1] Record the time at which the iodine stays orange-brown; repeat for pH 4 to 10
[1] Repeat each pH at least three times and calculate a mean to improve reliability (accept: use a control tube with water in place of amylase)
(e) [1] Safety: wear eye protection and wash off any iodine spills, or use a bench-level, sealed water bath, or avoid skin contact with buffers (any one sensible precaution)
[1] Ethics: if human saliva is used, use only the student's own saliva or a commercial enzyme, never share samples, and dispose of used samples hygienically (accept: obtain consent, no harm to others)
(f) [1] Plot a graph of the mean time (or rate = 1 ÷ time) against pH and read the pH with the fastest rate as the optimum
Common errors: listing 'the same pH' as a control; writing 'amylase dies' instead of 'denatures'; measuring starch left by eye without a defined end point; giving a hypothesis with no prediction.

questions.content:
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder in which thick mucus builds up in the lungs and digestive system. It is caused by a recessive allele (f). The normal allele is dominant (F). Two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis have a daughter who does have the disorder.

(a) State the genotype of the parents. (1 mark)
(b) Complete a Punnett square, or list the possible genotypes, for the offspring of these two parents. (2 marks)
(c) State the probability that their next child has cystic fibrosis. (1 mark)
(d) Calculate the probability that their next two children both do not have cystic fibrosis. (2 marks)
(e) Explain how a recessive allele can be present in a family for many generations without anyone having the disorder. (2 marks)
(f) The parents say: "We have had one child with cystic fibrosis, so our next three children will be fine." Evaluate this statement. (2 marks)
(g) Distinguish between the terms genotype and phenotype. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Both parents are Ff (heterozygous carriers)
(b) [1] Gametes shown correctly: F and f from each parent
[1] Offspring genotypes FF, Ff, Ff, ff (ratio 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff)
(c) [1] 1 in 4, or 25%, or 0.25
(d) [1] Probability of one child unaffected = 3/4 (0.75)
[1] 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16 or 0.5625 (accept 56% or 56.25%; ECF from their answer to (c), for example 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64)
(e) [1] Carriers (Ff) have one dominant allele F that produces enough working protein, so they do not show the disorder
[1] The recessive allele is passed on in gametes of carriers and only shows when two copies are inherited (ff)
(f) [1] The statement is incorrect because each child is an independent event, with the same 1 in 4 chance of the disorder each time
[1] The chance that all of the next three are unaffected is 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 = 0.42, so it is less than half, and an affected child remains possible (accept 27/64)
(g) [1] Genotype is the combination of alleles an organism has (for example Ff)
[1] Phenotype is the observable characteristic or trait that results from the genotype and the environment (for example having or not having the disorder)
Common errors: stating the probability of the next child as 'now 0 because we already had one'; adding probabilities instead of multiplying in (d); writing the Punnett square with the parents' gametes as ff and Ff.

questions.content:
A student measured her heart rate and stroke volume while resting and then after running on a treadmill for five minutes.

At rest: heart rate = 70 beats per minute, stroke volume = 70 cm³ per beat
After exercise: heart rate = 150 beats per minute, stroke volume = 100 cm³ per beat

Cardiac output (cm³ per minute) = heart rate × stroke volume

(a) Calculate the student's cardiac output at rest. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate her cardiac output after exercise. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in cardiac output caused by exercise. Give your answer to the nearest whole number. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why the heart rate increases during exercise. Link your answer to cell respiration. (3 marks)
(e) Compare the pressure and the route of blood in the pulmonary circuit and the systemic circuit. (2 marks)

(Total 10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 70 × 70
[1] 4900 cm³ per minute (units needed)
(b) [1] 150 × 100 = 15 000 cm³ per minute
(c) [1] (15 000 − 4900) ÷ 4900 × 100 (ECF from (a) and (b))
[1] 206% (accept 206.1; a final answer of 306% from dividing by the wrong value scores 0)
(d) [1] Muscles respire faster during exercise, so they need more oxygen and glucose
[1] A faster heartbeat increases blood flow, delivering oxygen and glucose to the muscles more quickly
[1] It also removes carbon dioxide and heat faster (accept: lactic acid removal)
(e) [1] Pulmonary circuit carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium at lower pressure
[1] Systemic circuit carries blood from the left ventricle around the body and back to the right atrium at higher pressure (the left ventricle has a thicker wall)
Common errors: omitting units; stating the increase as 10 100 cm³ per minute and stopping; saying the heart 'pumps oxygen'; confusing atria and ventricles.

questions.content:
A student investigated whether garlic extract can stop bacteria from growing. She spread a harmless bacterium evenly over the surface of an agar plate. She placed a paper disc soaked in garlic extract in the centre of one plate and recorded a clear zone of diameter 8 mm after incubating the plate for 48 hours. She did not set up any other plate. She concluded: "Garlic kills bacteria."

The student incubated the plate at 25 °C. The lid was taped shut with two pieces of tape and the plate was not opened after incubation.

(a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (2 marks)
(b) Identify two flaws in the design of the investigation. (2 marks)
(c) Explain why the plate was incubated at 25 °C with the lid taped, rather than at 37 °C with the lid open. (2 marks)
(d) Evaluate the validity of the student's conclusion. (3 marks)
(e) Suggest three improvements to the method that would make the results more valid and more reliable. (3 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Independent variable: the presence of garlic extract (or concentration of the extract)
[1] Dependent variable: diameter or area of the clear zone around the disc
(b) [1] No control: there was no plate with a disc soaked in water or a solvent only
[1] Only one plate and no repeats, so no mean can be calculated and reliability cannot be judged (accept: only one concentration tested)
(c) [1] 25 °C and a taped lid reduce the growth of dangerous pathogens that grow best at body temperature (37 °C)
[1] Taping prevents bacteria escaping into the room or contaminating the plate with other microbes, so the investigation is safe
(d) [1] The clear zone suggests the extract may stop growth, so the conclusion is partly supported
[1] The conclusion is not valid as stated: without a control the student cannot show the zone was caused by garlic and not by the disc, the solvent or the agar
[1] The zone shows growth was inhibited, not that bacteria were killed; this needs further testing, for example by transferring the bacteria to fresh agar
(e) [1] Add a control disc soaked in the same liquid without garlic, and a positive control with a known antibiotic
[1] Repeat with at least three plates and calculate the mean zone diameter
[1] Test several concentrations of extract with the same disc size, volume and agar depth, or use a sterile technique and measure with a ruler to the nearest millimetre in two directions (any three distinct improvements, one mark each)
Common errors: describing the control as 'the same bacteria'; stating that 25 °C is used because bacteria 'do not grow' at higher temperatures; saying the conclusion is 'wrong' without giving a reason.

questions.content:
A country is considering allowing farmers to grow a genetically modified (GM) maize. A gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis has been inserted into the maize so that it produces a protein that is toxic to a common caterpillar pest.

Data from field trials over one season:
Conventional maize: yield = 6.2 tonnes per hectare, insecticide sprays = 6 per season
GM maize: yield = 7.4 tonnes per hectare, insecticide sprays = 1 per season
Seed for the GM maize costs more than conventional seed. A typical farm in the region is 250 hectares.

(a) Calculate the percentage increase in yield for the GM maize compared with the conventional maize. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (2 marks)
(b) Calculate the extra maize, in tonnes, that a 250 hectare farm would produce if it grew GM maize. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of insecticide sprays. (1 mark)
(d) Describe how a gene from a bacterium can be transferred into a maize plant so that the maize produces the toxic protein. (2 marks)
(e) Evaluate whether the country should allow farmers to grow the GM maize. Consider environmental, economic and ethical impacts and reach a justified conclusion. (5 marks)
(f) State two limitations of the field trial data that should be considered before a final decision. (2 marks)

(Total 14 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] (7.4 − 6.2) ÷ 6.2 × 100
[1] 19.4% (3 significant figures; accept 19.35 if rounding shown)
(b) [1] Extra yield per hectare = 7.4 − 6.2 = 1.2 tonnes
[1] 1.2 × 250 = 300 tonnes
(c) [1] (6 − 1) ÷ 6 × 100 = 83.3% (accept 83%)
(d) [1] The gene is cut out of the bacterial DNA using restriction enzymes and inserted into a vector, such as a plasmid, or a gene gun is used
[1] The plant cells take up the gene, and the cells are grown into whole plants that make the protein (accept: ligase joins the gene to the DNA)
(e) [1] Environmental benefit: fewer insecticide sprays, so less harm to non-target insects, and pollution of water is reduced
[1] Environmental risk: pests may evolve resistance, or the gene may spread to wild relatives, reducing biodiversity
[1] Economic: higher yield (19.4%) and lower spray costs, but more expensive seed, so profit depends on the price of seed and maize
[1] Ethical or social: consider choice of farmers, labelling for consumers, ownership of seeds by companies, and long-term health safety testing
[1] A clear judgement supported by evidence from the data and at least one stated limitation or condition (for example: allow with monitoring and resistance management)
(f) [1] The trial lasted one season only, so long-term effects on resistance, soil and health are unknown
[1] Conditions may differ on other farms (soil, rainfall, pest levels), so the results may not apply everywhere (accept: no data on cost, no data on effects on other species)
Common errors: describing GM as 'adding chemicals'; giving only advantages; not using numbers from the data; concluding 'GM is bad' or 'GM is good' with no justification; reporting the percentage reduction as 5.

questions.content:
Human sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes. A fertility clinic provides information to couples about gametes and contraception.

A man produces about 60 million sperm cells per cm³ of semen. A typical sample of semen has a volume of 3.5 cm³.

(a) Name the type of cell division that produces gametes. (1 mark)
(b) State the number of chromosomes in a human sperm cell and in a human zygote. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the typical number of sperm cells in one sample of semen. Give your answer in millions. (2 marks)
(d) State where in the female reproductive system fertilisation usually occurs. (1 mark)
(e) Explain how the combined contraceptive pill reduces the chance of pregnancy. (2 marks)
(f) Two siblings have the same parents but are genetically different. Explain how meiosis and fertilisation produce this variation. (3 marks)

(Total 11 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] Meiosis
(b) [1] Sperm cell: 23 chromosomes
[1] Zygote: 46 chromosomes
(c) [1] 60 × 3.5
[1] 210 million (accept 210 000 000)
(d) [1] The oviduct (accept: fallopian tube)
(e) [1] It contains hormones (oestrogen and progesterone, or synthetic equivalents) that inhibit FSH and LH release
[1] This prevents the egg from maturing and ovulation from happening, so no egg is available to be fertilised (accept: thickens cervical mucus)
(f) [1] Independent assortment of chromosomes in meiosis gives different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in each gamete
[1] Crossing over exchanges sections of DNA between homologous chromosomes, producing new allele combinations
[1] Random fertilisation: any sperm can fuse with any egg, so each zygote has a unique combination of alleles
Common errors: stating that gametes have 46 chromosomes; confusing mitosis and meiosis; saying the pill 'kills sperm'; stating the number as 210 without units or the word million.
